evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database), Academia Sinica Character Database
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析; 喜 entry, graph analysis and cited inscriptions
evidence.text: The database analyzes oracle-bone and bronze 喜 as 壴 plus 口: 壴 is an early drum graph and 口 supplies the singing element in its proposed ‘drumming and singing for pleasure’ interpretation. It reports oracle-bone uses for names and for joy, citing 合集 15671「王其喜」and 21207「不喜」; bronze uses include names, a music term, joy in 井弔鐘「用喜樂文神人」, and a separate ritual reading 喜(饎) in 天亡簋「事喜(饎)上帝」. It provides corpus identifiers but no absolute dates for these examples. These are the database’s analyses and reported readings, not meanings directly visible in the shapes.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 喜

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析; 壴 entry
evidence.text: The database describes oracle-bone and bronze 壴 as an upright drum graph, with a top ornament, drum face and support; it says scholars commonly regard it as an early form of 鼓. It reports independent uses for beating a drum and musical terminology. This supports a semantic drum interpretation of the component, but does not establish壴 as a phonetic in 喜.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 壴

evidence.source: 中央研究院漢字構形資料庫 (Academia Sinica Character Database)
evidence.text: The page lists oracle-bone, bronze (including inscription index 集成04137), Chu manuscript, small-seal and Shuowen form categories. It proposes two interpretations for the graph: hearing drum music and smiling, or placing a drum on its stand to signal a festive event requiring music. These are proposed motivations, not a demonstrated chronological sequence of senses. The page states that its database content is All Rights Reserved.
evidence.title: 漢字「喜」：字形演變

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A00628; study notes for 喜, 憙 and 歖
evidence.text: The dictionary quotes Shuowen’s「喜，樂也。從壴從口」and distinguishes the separate entry 憙「說也。從心從喜，喜亦聲」, while noting later conflation of 憙 and 喜. It reports 歖 as Shuowen’s ancient-script form of 喜, formed with 欠. It also describes later altered 喜 shapes as scribal convenience or corruption, rather than evidence for the original graph. This is evidence about later graphic variants, not a dated sequence for the ancient graph.
evidence.title: [A00628] 喜 — Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: 許慎, 說文解字, transcribed in the Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The Shuowen entry glosses 喜 as joy and analyzes it as 从壴从口. This is an early lexicographic analysis of the graph, not independent proof that the proposed component motivation is historically correct. Its 歖 variant statement is discussed separately by the modern dictionary.
evidence.title: [A00628] 喜 — Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: character entry 喜; Shuowen quotation and Middle Chinese fanqie
evidence.text: The database records the Shuowen gloss and the Guangyun fanqie 虛里, assigning 喜 to the Middle Chinese 曉 initial, 上 tone, 之/止 rhyme, open division III. The supplied local Baxter–Sagart table separately gives 喜 MC xiX and OC *qʰ(r)əʔ; it gives 壴 MC trjuH and OC *t<r>oʔ-s. These distinct system-specific rows do not supply a clear sound match supporting 壴 as phonetic in 喜. Local provenance: sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv, rows 喜 and 壴; neither row is external evidence. The upstream character-data PDF could not be verified in this session.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 喜

Local primary data supplied in the packet give current kMandarin 喜 xǐ and 壴 zhù (sources/unihan/Unihan_Readings.txt, kMandarin rows 喜 and 壴); these are current metadata only, not evidence for an ancient sound relationship. The official character-specific records remain unavailable for citation in this run.

Opened character-specific entry and verified component analysis, traditional gloss, cited oracle-bone and bronze examples, and 壴’s independent drum-related evidence.

gaps: The cited oracle-bone witnesses are identified by corpus numbers, but the inspected sources do not give secure absolute dates for each example. The earliest attested sense therefore cannot be ranked precisely from these pages; joy/rejoicing and name uses are both reported in oracle-bone material.

Bronze 喜 is also reported for music terminology and a ritual reading written 喜(饎). The relation, if any, of that ritual use to ordinary joy is not established; it should not be presented as a semantic extension without further evidence.

The drum-and-singing interpretation is a specialist source’s reconstruction of graph motivation. Academia Sinica offers two possible explanations; neither source establishes a demonstrated chronology connecting the depicted action to the word’s senses. The inspected sources do not provide a full account of every early shape or demonstrate a specific corruption in 喜 itself.

No independently documented sound correspondence supports treating 壴 as the phonetic element in 喜. Exact local readings are available for both characters in Unihan and Baxter–Sagart tables, but the official per-character Unihan URLs and the upstream Baxter–Sagart data PDF could not be inspected; local rows are preserved as local provenance only.

Later ‘like/love/enjoy’ glosses occur in modern dictionary summaries, but the inspected historical evidence does not date or establish a semantic path from early joy to those senses. Shuowen separately records 憙 and 喜; later conflation is reported by the Taiwan variants dictionary.

Commons image descriptions establish candidate identity and rights, but the direct image fetches failed, so the glyph pixels were not visually inspected. The oracle and seal images are modern redrawings, not artifact photographs. No candidate image is available from the All Rights Reserved Academia Sinica graph-history page.
